raw_response:
I am 70 years old this year, and I have been farming my five mu of land in Quzhou County since I was a young man. My body is not as strong as it used to be, so I will not try anything risky. I know what this soil can do, and I will stick to the wheat-maize rotation that my family has relied on for generations. The groundwater table has dropped over the years, but my well still gives enough water for three or four irrigations on the wheat and two on the maize if I am careful.

This autumn, I will sow winter wheat after rotary tilling the land. I will use an improved variety like Luyuan 502 or Jimai 22 — not the old traditional seeds, because the improved ones give steadier yields and the seed dealer in town always has them in stock. I will put down compound fertilizer as basal dressing and topdress with urea in the spring. The wheat needs about three or four irrigations: the winter irrigation, the jointing water, and the grain-filling water. I will spray for aphids and diseases two or three times, and once for weeds. I expect around 1,000 jin per mu, maybe a bit more if the spring rain cooperates.

After harvesting the wheat in early June, I will plant maize right away without ploughing again — there is no time to waste, and no-tillage works fine if the wheat stubble is managed well. For maize, I trust Denghai 605; it is a hybrid that everyone around here grows because it stands up to wind and yields well. The maize only needs two irrigations, usually at the jointing and filling stages, and I will spray pesticides two or three times to control corn borers and weeds. If all goes well, I should get around 1,200 jin per mu.

I have thought about growing vegetables or cotton, but at my age I do not want the extra labor or the market risk. Wheat and maize have guaranteed buyers, and I can manage the work myself with some help from my nephew during busy times. Fertilizer prices have gone up, so I will use a moderate amount — enough to keep the yield but not so much that I waste money.
